blocks.overview: This case concerns Mr. Dhaliwal's judicial review of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) decision denying his claim of risk upon return to India due to perceived Khalistani Sikh separatist ties. Mr. Dhaliwal is the applicant appealing the PRRA officer's decision, and Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) is the respondent. The Federal Court found the PRRA decision unreasonable for ignoring key evidence and remitted the matter to a different decision-maker.

blocks.issue: Was the PRRA officer's decision reasonable given the evidence about Mr. Dhaliwal's risk as a perceived Sikh separatist?
blocks.court_conclusion: The decision is unreasonable due to ignoring key evidence and errors in risk assessment, lacking justification and transparency.

positions.text: Officer ignored risk profile as perceived Sikh separatist and failed to assess Indian authorities' likely actions if they discovered Canada's inadmissibility finding.
Sole issue is reasonableness; Officer presumed to have considered all evidence including CBSA 2023 Dossier in record.
Found insufficient evidence that Mr. Dhaliwal would be targeted or is a Khalistan supporter; rejected Ministerial relief applications.

propositions.text: Mr. Dhaliwal recanted previous statements about AISSF membership in 2009 Ministerial relief application under IRPA section 42.1
An exclusion order was issued in December 2023 for IRPA non-compliance
Mr. Dhaliwal received notice of entitlement to a PRRA after exclusion order
Mr. Dhaliwal asserted risk upon return to India due to perception as Khalistani Sikh separatist based on Canada's inadmissibility finding

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Dhaliwal recanted AISSF involvement in 2009, faced a 2023 exclusion order, received PRRA notice, and claimed risk as a perceived Khalistani separatist.

propositions.text: PRRA officer found Mr. Dhaliwal's assumption of Indian government seeking Canadian info speculative
Officer found insufficient evidence that Mr. Dhaliwal would be targeted due to Canadian Federal Court cases
Officer found insufficient evidence that Mr. Dhaliwal is or will be targeted for Khalistan support
Officer found insufficient evidence of Mr. Dhaliwal's status as Khalistan supporter
Mr. Dhaliwal seeks judicial review of PRRA Decision

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA officer found Mr. Dhaliwal's risk assumptions speculative and evidence insufficient; Mr. Dhaliwal seeks judicial review of this Decision, court states.

propositions.text: The Decision is unreasonable after considering parties' submissions
Mr. Dhaliwal rebutted presumption that Officer considered all material, especially key evidence
Deference to decision-maker does not apply when evidence is ignored
Judicial review application granted; matter remitted to different decision-maker

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Decision unreasonable, Mr. Dhaliwal rebutted presumption of full consideration, denies deference, grants judicial review, and remits matter.

propositions.text: Court will outline Mr. Dhaliwal's immigration history and analysis leading to judicial review grant

paragraphs.summary: The court will outline Mr. Dhaliwal's immigration history and analysis leading to judicial review grant.

propositions.text: Mr. Dhaliwal left India in 1991, traveled to Brazil for two months, then to US claiming asylum based on AISSF membership fear
Before US refugee claim decision, Mr. Dhaliwal came to Canada and filed refugee claim on same risk
Mr. Dhaliwal abandoned Canadian refugee claim after marrying Canadian citizen
Spousal sponsorship application was submitted then withdrawn after divorce

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Dhaliwal fled India in 1991, sought asylum in US and Canada, abandoned claim after marriage, and withdrew spousal sponsorship after divorce.

propositions.text: Mr. Dhaliwal was granted several TRPs starting in 1993
Married current spouse in 1998; subsequent spousal sponsorship rejected due to impaired driving conviction
Paragraph 34(1)(f) inadmissibility found in 2006 after third spousal sponsorship and interviews about AISSF involvement
No evidence of judicial review challenge to inadmissibility determination

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Dhaliwal received TRPs since 1993, married current spouse in 1998, faced inadmissibility in 2006, and no judicial review challenged it.

propositions.text: Mr. Dhaliwal sought Ministerial relief under IRPA subsection 34(2) recanting AISSF involvement
Ministerial relief application was rejected
Mr. Dhaliwal sought judicial review and was granted leave
Matter remitted for redetermination on consent
Ministerial relief refused again on redetermination and subsequent judicial review application

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Dhaliwal sought Ministerial relief recanting AISSF involvement, was rejected, obtained judicial review leave, matter remitted, relief refused again.

propositions.text: Mr. Dhaliwal obtained at least one Indian passport valid 2009-2019

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Dhaliwal held an Indian passport valid from 2009 to 2019.

propositions.text: Mr. Dhaliwal applied for TRPs before 2012 expiry; applications refused including last in 2014 partly due to inadmissibility
Last TRP refusal was subject of Dhaliwal 2015 decision
Despite refusals, Mr. Dhaliwal remained in Canada with work permits

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Dhaliwal's TRP applications were refused including in 2014, subject to 2015 decision, but he remained in Canada with work permits.

propositions.text: CBSA provided Mr. Dhaliwal draft recommendations and opportunity to comment on Ministerial relief requests
Mr. Dhaliwal sought Ministerial relief third time in 2023; CBSA gave negative draft recommendation
Minister denied relief again in 2025
Latest rejection is subject of pending judicial review scheduled for September 29, 2025

paragraphs.summary: The court states CBSA gave draft recommendations on Ministerial relief, Mr. Dhaliwal sought relief in 2023, Minister denied in 2025, pending judicial review scheduled.

propositions.text: Mr. Dhaliwal voluntarily submitted PRRA application in 2016, not processed as no removal order existed

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Dhaliwal submitted a PRRA application in 2016 which was not processed due to no removal order.

propositions.text: Exclusion Order made December 8, 2023 for IRPA non-compliance
Mr. Dhaliwal notified same day of entitlement to submit PRRA application
PRRA rejection is subject of current judicial review application

paragraphs.summary: The court states an Exclusion Order was made December 8, 2023, Mr. Dhaliwal notified of PRRA entitlement, and PRRA rejection is under judicial review.

propositions.text: Mr. Dhaliwal met burden showing the Decision is unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Dhaliwal met his burden to show the Decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Reasonableness standard of review applies; decision must show justification, transparency, intelligibility
Decision may be unreasonable if decision-maker misapprehended evidence
Challenger has onus to prove unreasonableness: Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 paras 10,25,99-100,125-126

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonableness standard applies, decision must be justified, misapprehension can cause unreasonableness, challenger bears onus per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Did Officer ignore risk profile as perceived Sikh separatist despite evidence Indian authorities can find Canadian AISSF finding?
Did Officer fail to assess Indian authorities' likely actions if they discovered Canada found Applicant a banned Sikh separatist?

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Dhaliwal frames issues whether Officer ignored risk profile as Sikh separatist and failed to assess Indian authorities' likely actions.

propositions.text: Sole issue is reasonableness of the Decision
Court agrees sole issue is reasonableness; reformulation unnecessary as outcome depends on reasonableness

paragraphs.summary: The respondent says sole issue is reasonableness; court agrees and finds reformulation unnecessary as outcome depends on reasonableness.

propositions.text: Counsel argued Officer failed to mention CBSA 2023 Dossier heavily relied on in PRRA submissions

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Dhaliwal's counsel argued Officer failed to mention CBSA 2023 Dossier heavily relied on in PRRA submissions.

propositions.text: Officer presumed to have considered all evidence before them
CBSA 2023 Dossier was before Officer as included in certified tribunal record

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Officer presumed to consider all evidence and CBSA 2023 Dossier was before Officer in tribunal record.

propositions.text: Officer not obligated to mention every piece of evidence or how dealt with: Cepeda-Gutierrez 1998 FC para 16
More important unmentioned evidence may lead court to infer erroneous finding without regard to evidence: Cepeda para 17

paragraphs.summary: The court states Officer need not mention all evidence but important unmentioned evidence may imply erroneous findings per Cepeda.

propositions.text: Presumption Officer considered all evidence rebutted by Decision itself
Officer stated evidence submitted and considered: NDP, articles on Sikhs targeted, documents on Karanbir Singh, public court cases

paragraphs.summary: The court finds presumption Officer considered all evidence rebutted by Decision, which lists considered evidence including NDP and public court cases.

propositions.text: The CBSA 2023 Dossier is not included in the Officer's reasons as per the Court's view.
In Cepeda, if an agency refers to evidence supporting its finding but is silent on contradictory evidence, it may have overlooked the contradictory evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the CBSA 2023 Dossier was not included in the Officer's reasons and cites Cepeda on overlooking contradictory evidence.

propositions.text: The CBSA 2023 Dossier contradicts the Officer's finding about Mr. Dhaliwal's involvement and risk as a Khalistan supporter.
The Officer found limited evidence of applicant's involvement and risk, but the CBSA 2023 Dossier shows long involvement and recanting of initial narrative.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the CBSA 2023 Dossier contradicts the Officer's finding; the court summarizes the Officer's finding and dossier content.

propositions.text: The CBSA 2023 Dossier was so important that the Officer's failure to mention it implies the finding was made without regard to it.
Paraphrasing Cepeda, failure to mention important evidence allows inference of overlooking it.
The Officer considered other evidence and accepted discrimination against Khalistan supporters but found insufficient evidence linking applicant to risks under IRPA sections 96 and 97.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer overlooked the important CBSA 2023 Dossier, relying on Cepeda, and notes the Officer's other findings on evidence and risk.

propositions.text: Cepeda acknowledged omission of discussion of reports may not vitiate decision if the report is at least acknowledged.
Here, the Officer did not mention the CBSA 2023 Dossier, so the omission justifies granting judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Cepeda allows omission if report acknowledged, but here the Officer did not mention the dossier, justifying judicial review.

propositions.text: The Officer erred by considering section 96 IRPA when only limited PRRA with section 97 risk assessment applied.
Vavilov states minor errors alone may not warrant intervention.
Combined with omission of CBSA 2023 Dossier, the Decision is unreasonable for lacking justification, transparency, and intelligibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer erred on IRPA section, cites Vavilov on minor errors, and concludes the Decision is unreasonable due to combined errors.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is granted and the matter is remitted to a different decision-maker for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review and remits the matter to a different decision-maker for redetermination.

propositions.text: No serious question of general importance arises for certification from either party.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious question of general importance arises for certification.
